instructions:
Start every session with whats_waiting: it is the queue of what your person's Vexa needs right now, and for a new person it holds their first step. Follow what it says before anything else.

Vexa puts a transcription bot into a live meeting (Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, Zoom, Jitsi) and gives you the transcript while the meeting is still running.

The canonical flow:
  1. parse_meeting_link(meeting_url)  → platform + native_meeting_id (pure; no side effects)
  2. request_meeting_bot(meeting_url) → sends the bot. A human in the meeting must ADMIT it, so
     expect a delay between `requested` and `active`.
  3. get_meeting_transcript(platform, native_meeting_id) → segments, WHILE the meeting runs.
     Poll it to follow a live meeting; pass `since_index` to get only what is new since your last
     call instead of re-reading the whole transcript. Answers come in pages (`limit`, default 200;
     `until_index` caps the range): while `has_more` is true, call again with since_index=next_index.
  4. stop_bot(platform, native_meeting_id) when you are done.

Identity: every tool returns `platform` + `native_meeting_id`, and every tool accepts those same two names. Feed one tool's output straight into the next.

Signed-in bots: a meeting that admits only signed-in users needs a bot account. bot_accounts_list shows the saved ones; pass a usable `id` as request_meeting_bot's `bot_account`. To add or repair one, browser_session_open opens a live browser in which the PERSON signs in themselves; never ask for or type a password.

Make the data yours: annotate_meeting attaches a title and arbitrary metadata — a CRM id, a ticket, tags, your own summary — to a meeting, DURING it or after it ended. Anything you put there you can find again with list_meetings(metadata_filter={...}), searched in the database rather than on one page. If you learn something durable about a meeting, write it back; that is what lets the next agent (or the next you) pick it up.

The bot is a PARTICIPANT, not just a recorder: get_meeting_chat reads the in-call chat, and speak_in_meeting says something out loud to everyone present. Speaking is irreversible and visible to real people — do it only when the person you work for asked you to say that thing, never to test and never on your own initiative.

A meeting with status `active` and zero segments usually means the bot has not been admitted yet, or nobody has spoken — it does not mean transcription is broken.

vexa.meeting_prep.description: Meeting prep flow using Vexa MCP tools.

content.text:
You are helping me prepare a meeting using Vexa.

Goals:
1. Identify meeting platform + native meeting id (+ passcode if needed).
2. Request the meeting bot (idempotent).

Rules:
- Prefer calling `parse_meeting_link` when `meeting_url` is provided.
- When requesting a bot, pass `meeting_url` if you have it; otherwise use `native_meeting_id` (+ `passcode` for Teams, from ?p=).
- Keep any provided notes in the conversation for the post-meeting summary (storing notes on the meeting record is not available via this MCP yet).

Input:
- meeting_url: �meeting_url�
- platform: �platform�
- native_meeting_id: �native_meeting_id�
- notes: �notes�

Now do the tool calls and tell me what you did and what to do next.

vexa.during_meeting.description: During-meeting helper prompt using Vexa MCP tools.

content.text:
You are my during-meeting assistant using Vexa.

Meeting: platform=�platform�, id=�native_meeting_id�

Steps:
- Call `get_bot_status` to confirm the bot is active / requested.
- Call `get_meeting_transcript` to fetch the current transcript snapshot.
- If the transcript is empty, explain whether the meeting may not have started, bot may not be admitted yet, or transcription isn't producing segments.

Then summarize key points and action items so far.

You are my post-meeting assistant using Vexa.

Steps:
- Call `get_meeting_transcript` to fetch the meeting status, notes, and segments.
- Call `list_recordings` (optionally `get_recording`) if recordings are expected.
- Produce:
  1) concise summary
  2) decisions
  3) action items with owners (if known) and due dates (if mentioned)
  4) open questions

Help me troubleshoot a Microsoft Teams meeting link for Vexa.

User link: �meeting_url�

Checklist:
- If link is `teams.live.com/meet/<id>?p=<passcode>`:
  - native_meeting_id = <id> (10-17 digits)
  - passcode = value of ?p= (often required)
  - Prefer using `meeting_url` directly with `request_meeting_bot`.
- Enterprise `teams.microsoft.com/meet/<id>?p=<passcode>` short links are supported; legacy `/l/meetup-join/...` links are forwarded as raw URLs.
- If passcode fails validation, explain constraints (8-20 alphanumeric) and ask for a corrected link.

If a link is provided, call `parse_meeting_link` and show the extracted fields.

tools.name: parse_meeting_link
tools.description:
Parse Meeting Link

Parse a meeting URL into platform/native_meeting_id/passcode.

{

tools.description:
Request Meeting Bot

Request a Vexa bot to join a meeting for transcription.

Provide meeting_url OR native_meeting_id (+ platform, + passcode for Teams).
Note: after a successful request, it typically takes about 10 seconds for the bot to join.
Sent from a chat, that chat is the meeting's chat: its live transcript, the post-meeting
notes and proposals come there, not to a separate meeting chat.

tools.name: get_meeting_transcript
tools.description:
Get Meeting Transcript

Get the transcript for a meeting (segments with speaker, timestamp, text). Works DURING the
meeting as well as after — poll it to follow a live one.

Identify the meeting with `platform` + `native_meeting_id` — the exact field names
request_meeting_bot, list_meetings and parse_meeting_link hand back — or with
`meeting_db_id` for ONE exact past meeting. The pair names the ROOM, so on a recurring
link it returns the NEWEST session held there; `meeting_db_id` never moves.

To follow a live meeting cheaply, pass `since_index` = the `next_index` from your previous
call; you get only what has been said since, instead of the whole transcript every time.

Paging: one answer carries at most `limit` segments (default and maximum 200) from
`since_index` up to, not including, `until_index`. `has_more` is true when the range you
asked for continues past this page; call again with since_index=`next_index` (same
`until_index`) to get the rest. `complete` is true only when you have reached the end of
the whole transcript. Never summarise from a page while `has_more` or `complete` says
there is more.

### Responses:

**200**: Successful Response (Success Response)
Content-Type: application/json

native_meeting_id.description: The meeting's native id — exactly the `native_meeting_id` returned by request_meeting_bot, list_meetings or parse_meeting_link (e.g. 'abc-defg-hij' for Google Meet).

platform.title: platform

meeting_db_id.description: The meeting's exact database row id — the `meeting_db_id` (or `id`) that list_meetings, request_meeting_bot, annotate_meeting and search_transcripts return. Takes precedence over `platform` + `native_meeting_id`, which name the ROOM and therefore resolve to the NEWEST meeting held on that link. Use it whenever you mean one specific past meeting.
meeting_db_id.title: meeting_db_id

since_index.description: Return only segments at or after this index. Pass the `next_index` from your previous call to follow a live meeting without re-reading what you already have.
since_index.title: since_index

limit.description: Most segments to return in this page (1-200, default 200). Ask for a small page when you only need part of a long meeting; `has_more` and `next_index` tell you how to get the rest.
limit.title: limit

until_index.description: Stop before this segment index (exclusive upper bound). With `since_index` it reads one fixed range, e.g. since_index=100&until_index=150.

Search Transcripts

Search what was SAID across your meetings. Use this instead of pulling transcripts and
reading them — it returns ranked snippets, not whole transcripts.

Each hit carries the meeting's `platform` + `native_meeting_id`, the speaker, the
timestamp, and a snippet with the match wrapped in <mark> tags. Feed those identity fields
straight into get_meeting_transcript when you need the full context around a hit.

This is lexical search with stemming, not semantic: "renewal" finds "renewals" but will
NOT find "extend the contract". Search the words people actually said.

tools.name: annotate_meeting
tools.description:
Annotate Meeting

Set the meeting's title and/or attach arbitrary metadata to it. Works DURING a live meeting
and after it has ended.

To annotate ONE PAST meeting, pass `meeting_db_id`. `platform` + `native_meeting_id` name
the ROOM, and a recurring link is the same room every week, so the pair always writes to
the NEWEST meeting held there — which is not the one you just read if you read an older
one.

`metadata` is your own JSON — a CRM id, a ticket, tags, your own summary, anything.
It always MERGES key-wise, and sending a key as null deletes exactly that key. You can
only ever affect keys you name: other agents and the human may have written annotations
here that you cannot see, and nothing you send can destroy them.

Find these meetings again with
`list_meetings(metadata_filter='{"your_key":"your_value"}')` — note the filter is a JSON
STRING, not an object.

tools.name: browser_session_open
tools.description:
Browser Session Open

Open a live browser in which the person signs a bot account in to Google, Microsoft or Zoom.

Use it when a meeting only admits signed-in users, when the person asks to set up a
signed-in bot, or when bot_accounts_list shows an account as 'signed_out' (pass its
`account_id` to sign it in again). The person types their own credentials in the live view;
you never ask for, receive or type a password, and you never try to drive the sign-in.

The result carries `ui_action: "open_browser_session"` and the session fields
(`session_id`, `vnc_password`, `platform`, `view_path`, `ws_path`, `expires_at`): a Vexa
client opens the live view from them. Tell the person a browser window has opened for them
to sign in. When they are done the account is saved; call bot_accounts_list to see it, then
pass its `id` as `bot_account` to request_meeting_bot.

### Responses:

**200**: Successful Response (Success Response)
Content-Type: application/json

platform.description: Which sign-in the browser opens on: 'google' (Google Meet), 'microsoft' (Teams), 'zoom' (Zoom).

display_name.description: A name for the saved account, e.g. 'Sales notetaker'. Optional.

owner.title: owner
owner.description: 'me' (default) saves the account for the person only; 'company' saves it for everyone in the company, where the company allows it.

account_id.title: account_id
account_id.description: Sign an EXISTING bot account in again (an `id` from bot_accounts_list, typically one whose state is 'signed_out'). Omit to create a new account.

tools.name: bot_accounts_list
tools.description:
Bot Accounts List

List the signed-in bot accounts this person can send to meetings: their own and the
company's. Wraps: GET /bot-accounts

Each account has `id`, `platform` (google | microsoft | zoom), `display_name`, `owner`,
`state` ('ok' or 'signed_out'), `verified_at`, `usable` (whether this person may send it)
and `mine`. Pass a usable account's `id` as `bot_account` to request_meeting_bot. A
'signed_out' account needs the person to sign in again: browser_session_open with its
`account_id`.

### Responses:

**200**: Successful Response (Success Response)
Content-Type: application/json

tools.name: bot_account_verify
tools.description:
Bot Account Verify

Check that a saved bot account is still signed in. Wraps: POST /bot-accounts/{account_id}/verify

The check runs in the background and answers `{account_id, check_id, status: "checking"}`
at once; call bot_accounts_list after a minute or so to read the account's new `state` and
`verified_at`. Use it before relying on an account that has not been verified recently.

### Responses:

**200**: Successful Response (Success Response)
Content-Type: application/json

tools.name: report_issue
tools.description:
Report Issue

Tell the Vexa maintainers that something went wrong. A human reads every ticket, and it cannot be withdrawn.

Call this the moment you hit a problem with Vexa — you do not need to have solved it first:
- something BROKE: an error, a bot that never joined, an empty transcript, a call that hung;
- something was CONFUSING: docs or an error message left you guessing which argument to send;
- something is MISSING: the capability you needed does not exist in the API.

A workaround you had to invent is worth filing too — that is the report we most want.
Write what you tried and what happened in your own words. Do not paste API keys, and do not
paste your user's meeting content.

File only when you hit this while doing REAL WORK for someone. If you are exploring,
evaluating or testing this API, do not file — write your findings in your report instead.
A ticket reaches humans at another company and cannot be withdrawn, and an evaluation run
can otherwise open several in a single session.

If the issue concerns a meeting or a bot, include `native_meeting_id` and `platform`. That is the
join key: it lines your account of what happened up against our own record of the same
meeting, which is the difference between a complaint and something we can diagnose. The
meeting is resolved onto the ticket only if the key you are calling with owns it.

Put links, if you have them, in the text — nothing you send here is ever fetched by us.

One-way: nothing auto-replies and nothing auto-closes. Returns the ticket
(`id` · `status` · `severity` · `opened` · `opened_by` · `entity`), plus `url` when the
deployment's sink issues one — tell your human where the report landed. On a deployment
with no ticket sink configured it returns 503 and nothing else is affected.

### Responses:

**200**: Successful Response (Success Response)
Content-Type: application/json
